item.source_locator: Ch. 4, section 'The Cultural Construction of Meaning', printed pp. 193-194
item.question: What contrast does the source draw between Indian and contemporary Western posters, and what reason does it give for the Indian side of it?
item.answer: Western posters present a dramatic enigma — provocative images and text giving incomplete or paradoxical information — which the public must see the film to resolve, and they are supported substantially by text, including review quotations that function as 'the media seal of approval' plus studio, producer and director credits signalling the film's status. Indian posters 'rarely use text'. The reason given is distribution: with the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, 'text is seen as a cultural barrier' — text picks a language, and picking a language cuts the audience. From the 1980s it has been more common for only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director to appear, printed solely in English, because to the public those three figures are themselves a marker of the style, content and quality of the film.
item.support: 'text is seen as a cultural barrier'
item.confounders: The absence of text is not an aesthetic preference in this account; it is a response to a multilingual distribution constraint, and the three names that DO appear are doing the work the review quotations do elsewhere.

item.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
item.source_locator: printed p. 34, 'Think small'; and printed p. 35, the Sugoi applications
item.question: A client insists the mark will only ever appear on a website and on large exhibition panels, so small-size behaviour does not matter. What is Airey's argument against accepting that, and what is his commercial argument rather than his aesthetic one?
item.answer: His argument is that the ambition to see work on billboards is exactly what makes designers forget the other end, and that the design may also need to accommodate smaller applications — his named cases are zip pulls and clothing labels, and the Sugoi mark is photographed on both a zip pull and a woven garment label. His commercial argument, which is the one to put to a client, is not about craft: an adaptable mark saves the client a considerable amount of money on print costs, brand-application meetings and potential redesigns, which is why he says clients are typically enthusiastic about and demanding of adaptability. Note the honest limit — he never quantifies that saving. Note also what your client is really asserting: that the set of future applications is known now, which is the assumption an identity designed to last the lifetime of the company cannot safely make.
item.support: Printed p. 34 for the argument and the client-cost reasoning; printed p. 35 for the Sugoi applications, which were rendered and inspected during extraction. The cost saving is asserted and never quantified.
confounders: arguing only from craft, which gives the client nothing to weigh
citing the one-inch figure as a standard rather than as this author's rule of thumb
assuming a favicon is the small case he has in mind; his small cases are physical merchandise

item.source_locator: Ch. 3 'The Art of Advertising', printed pp. 101-182; thesis stated at p. 101
item.question: What is chapter 3's organising claim about how film-advertising style changed, and why does the Art Deco phase matter to that claim?
item.answer: That Indian film advertising did not evolve toward a single style but moved through distinct phases, each borrowing 'the aesthetic vocabulary of the period'. The sequence given: text-only newspaper notices and handbills from 1896; the Ravi Varma aesthetic, realist oil technique on Hindu mythological subject matter, carried into posters via the Varma press's oleographs; the Bombay School of Art style, a delicate realism tied to the Ajanta revival, used when a studio wanted to signal a film was special; Art Deco from the 1930s as a universal symbol of modernity; nationalist imagery around Independence, often using the map of India; overpainted montage in the 1970s-80s; computer-aided design from the 1990s. Art Deco matters because of how it ended: it 'did not survive beyond the end of the 1940s' in India because it came to be seen as Western cultural imperialism. That is a style displaced by a political meaning attaching to it rather than by a better style, which is the strongest evidence for the chapter's claim that these are period vocabularies rather than steps toward a solution.
item.support: each phase borrows 'the aesthetic vocabulary of the period'; Art Deco 'did not survive beyond the end of the 1940s'
item.confounders: Read as a progression toward better design, the sequence supports a 'this is how you make a film poster' conclusion. Read as the source states it, it supports the opposite: no phase here is the answer.

source_terms: ask your client very early whether a print budget has been set, since colour usually costs more and can limit the scope of your design
your multicoloured rainbow effect will cost more to produce than, say, a cool monotone grey design
item.claim: The source makes the client's print budget a design constraint to be discovered before designing, not a production detail to be handled afterwards: colour usually costs more and can limit the scope of the design. It gives the concrete case — a company that promotes itself through leaflets at trade events can be reminded that a multicoloured effect will cost more to produce than a monotone one. It also warns that every printer's pricing is different: with some printers, full-colour costs come close to one-colour jobs, but this is usually infrequent. The source assigns the duty to the designer — it is your job to inform the client about commercial printing requirements and limitations early in the process.

mechanism.text: Colour count drives commercial print cost, and print volume is where an identity's ongoing cost lives, so a colour decision taken without knowing the budget can commit the client to a cost they did not agree to.

scope.conditions: clients with significant commercial print volume; the source's frame is trade-show leaflets and corporate stationery around 2010

caveats.text: this is physical print economics, tied to 2010 commercial printing. It is production knowledge in the source's own frame and must not be rewritten as an instruction to any generative process.
the source explicitly declines to give figures and says every printer's prices are unique

source_stated_problems: a colour scheme the client cannot afford to print
a design decision that raises the client's ongoing production cost
source_stated_remedies: ask about the print budget very early
inform the client about commercial print requirements and limitations at the start

item.source_locator: Ch. 4, section 'The Cultural Construction of Meaning', printed pp. 193-194
item.question: A distributor must design one key art for a film releasing simultaneously in six Indian language markets and in three diaspora territories. What does this source's account of text actually argue, and where does the argument stop being about India in 2002?
item.answer: The argument is not that posters look better without text; it is that TEXT PICKS A LANGUAGE AND PICKING A LANGUAGE CUTS THE AUDIENCE. With the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, 'text is seen as a cultural barrier', which is why Indian posters 'rarely use text' while contemporary Western posters carry substantial copy including review quotations acting as 'the media seal of approval'. So the reasoning transfers exactly to the case described: one artwork across nine markets is precisely the condition the convention was a response to, and every word added narrows it. What the source also supplies is what replaced the text — from the 1980s only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director, printed solely in English, because to the public those three names themselves signal the style, content and quality of the film. That second half is where the transfer stops. It depends on a star-and-credit system in which those three names carry meaning to that public, which is a fact about Indian audiences in a particular period and not a general property of names. In a diaspora territory whose audience does not hold that system, removing the text removes the signal and does not replace it, and the source says nothing about what would. Nothing here is measured either: no comparison of a text-carrying and a text-free poster is reported anywhere in the book.
item.support: 'text is seen as a cultural barrier'
item.confounders: Treating this as a minimalist design principle inverts it. The convention is a distribution constraint, and in a single-language market the constraint is absent.

source_terms: Get to the heart of the story faster, and use engaging pacing and tight framing to draw viewers in
item.claim: The source's named technique "Jump in" asks the ad to reach the heart of its story sooner than it otherwise would, and names two specific means of doing so: pacing that keeps the viewer engaged, and tight framing.

scope.conditions: Named as a core Attention guideline, before any objective-specific tailoring

caveats.text: "Faster" is comparative with no stated reference point, and the source gives no target time to the heart of the story. The instruction is directional only.
Tight framing is asserted, not explained. The source gives no mechanism for why tighter framing draws viewers in.

Platform- and time-contingent. This is guidance about one company's ad products on one platform. Playback behaviour, ad formats and surfaces change; the source does not claim a durable mechanism and none should be read in.

Declared publisher interest. The publisher sells advertising on the platform whose creative guidance this is, and the cited research validates that product. Third-party involvement (Ipsos as research partner; Nielsen and Kantar as independent reviewers, per the source's own account) moderates this; it does not remove it.

item.question: You are asked to build an automated check for the source's "Jump in" guideline. Why can it not be run on individual frames, and what does the source fail to give you?
item.answer: Because what "Jump in" describes is a property of a span, not of a still: how quickly the ad reaches the heart of its story, and whether the pacing and framing across the opening draw the viewer in. No single frame carries any of that, so the unit of observation has to be the opening sequence at least. What the source fails to give you is every number the check would need — no target time to the heart of the story, no definition of what the heart of the story is, and no reference point for "faster", which is comparative with nothing to compare to. The only figure anywhere nearby is a five-second mention in an illustrative caption about when one ad introduced its brand, which is a different guideline and is not stated as a rule. A check built from this can be directional; any threshold in it is the implementer's.

source_terms: It understands that there are no final solutions to problems; at best there is a temporary equilibrium that must eventually get destabilized and give way to a new equilibrium.
keeping a solution perfect will take an ever increasing amount of effort that eventually becomes unsustainable
item.claim: Desai's most explicitly argued thesis is that the Indian disposition to accept the almost-good-enough — usually deplored as *chalta hai* — encodes a defensible position about time: that solutions are temporary equilibria, that imperfection is a permanent condition conferred by time, and that holding a solution perfect costs ever-increasing effort until it becomes unsustainable. He contrasts this with what he characterises as a Western analytical mode that reduces a problem to components and freezes it in time, taking the individual as the fundamental unit.
item.interpretation_basis: This is a thesis, not an observation. It is argued by assertion and by illustration from Indian political leadership, and its central contrast — "the Indian mind" versus "Western analysis" — is a pair of essayistic generalisations for which no evidence of any kind is offered.

mechanism.text: Maintaining any solution against a changing environment requires continuing effort that rises as the environment diverges from the one the solution was built for. A solution treated as final therefore becomes more expensive to hold indefinitely.

scope.conditions: The author's thesis about a disposition he attributes to India, illustrated from Indian political leadership of the 1990s-2000s (Vajpayee, Manmohan Singh) and contrasted with the United States under one administration.

caveats.text: 'the Indian mind' and 'Western analysis' are essayistic abstractions. This object records that DESAI ARGUES this. It is not evidence that Indians or Westerners think in these ways, and must never be consumed as a description of any population
the maintenance-cost mechanism is separable from the cultural thesis and is the only part with any general force; the cultural attribution is the part with none
the author anticipates the objection that this is an argument for passivity and answers it rhetorically rather than with evidence
this is the single object in this file most at risk of being universalised, which is why the risk is stated on the object itself

source_stated_problems: treating every situation as a problem awaiting a final solution
source_stated_remedies: the author proposes moving 'beyond the simplistic problem/solution mode into the process/time mode' — a posture, not a procedure

provenance.chapter: The Power of the Imperfect Solution
provenance.locator: Essay 'The Power of the Imperfect Solution', ch.5 'The Patterns Within' (spine 48)

source_terms: He has almost never seen a commercial shorter than two minutes produce profitable sales.
You must allow 20 seconds to give information on how to order.
These marathon commercials don't seem to irritate people as much as a cluster of short ones – 'like five salesmen knocking on the door, one after another.'
The demonstrations should promise not one benefit, but several. (This runs counter to the Procter & Gamble formula.)
item.claim: Television that asks for a direct order is described as a different craft from television that builds a brand. The right kind of commercial sets up a problem and demonstrates the product solving it, gives a money-back guarantee, includes the price, and asks for the order explicitly and urgently. The demonstration should promise several benefits rather than one — and the source flags himself that this runs counter to the single-benefit formula he praises in his chapter on Procter & Gamble. Length is treated as a requirement: his most experienced colleague has almost never seen a commercial shorter than two minutes produce profitable sales, and twenty seconds must be allowed purely for ordering information, long enough to give a toll-free number and a post office box with supers and to repeat the number at least twice. He reports that long commercials seem to irritate people less than a cluster of short ones.

mechanism.text: The commercial must complete a sale rather than start one, so it has to carry the demonstration, the guarantee, the price, the ask and the ordering mechanics — and that content sets a floor on the length.

scope.conditions: commercials asking for orders by mail or telephone, in the broadcast environment of the period

caveats.text: the several-benefits instruction directly opposes the single-benefit rule the source endorses elsewhere in the same book, and he marks the conflict himself without resolving it. The two are stated for different objectives — completing a sale versus building a brand — which is the reconciliation available but not the one he gives
the two-minute floor is attributed to one colleague's experience, not to a test
the twenty seconds of ordering information is a requirement of 1983 telephone and mail ordering and belongs to that infrastructure

source_stated_remedies: set up a problem, demonstrate the solution, guarantee, price it, and ask for the order
allow twenty seconds for ordering information

intra_source_relations.note: the single-benefit rule the source praises in the Procter & Gamble chapter
problem-solution used where the measure is orders
